paragraphs.heading: Two molecules become one
paragraphs.text: In an addition reaction, two or more molecules join together to make one larger molecule. That combined product has its own name: the adduct. Addition is the reverse of an elimination reaction, where a single molecule breaks apart into two or more.

paragraphs.heading: Which molecules can add
paragraphs.text: Only compounds with multiple bonds can take part in an addition reaction. An alkene, which has a double bond between two carbon atoms, qualifies, and so does an alkyne, which has a triple bond. Compounds with rings can count too, because rings are also treated as points of unsaturation. So can molecules with a double bond between carbon and a heteroatom, such as the carbonyl group, C=O, or the imine group, C=N, because of that double bond.

paragraphs.heading: Water meets an alkene
paragraphs.text: Hydration gives a concrete picture. An alkene, with its carbon–carbon double bond, takes part in an addition reaction with water, and the two combine into a single, larger molecule: an alcohol. That alcohol is the adduct. Run the change backwards, by dehydration, and the alcohol is turned back into the alkene, which makes the reverse an elimination reaction.

paragraphs.heading: Polar and non-polar kinds
paragraphs.text: Chemists sort addition reactions into polar and non-polar kinds. There are two main polar types: electrophilic addition and nucleophilic addition. Alongside them sit two non-polar types, called free-radical addition and cycloadditions. Addition reactions also turn up when polymers are made, and there the process goes by the name addition polymerization.

paragraphs.heading: When the adduct reacts again
paragraphs.text: The adduct is not always the end of the story. Depending on how its structure is built, it may react again right away and throw out a leaving group. That two-part path, an addition followed at once by an elimination, is known as the addition–elimination sequence. It ties together the two opposite reaction types: first two molecules combine into one, and then that one splits apart again.
